title: The linear syzygies of two polynomial variables
statement: Let $k$ be a field and $S=k[x_0,x_1]$ with the standard grading [def-sc-p1-standard] [def-pc-standard-graded-algebra]. If $a,b\in S$ satisfy $a x_0+b x_1=0$, then there is $c\in S$ with $a=c x_1$ and $b=-c x_0$.

source.place: proof of the Koszul resolution on the regular sequence x_0,x_1; the elementary two-variable syzygy calculation is expanded here

proof.text: View S as the polynomial ring k[x_1][x_0]. Write b=b_0+x_0b_1 with b_0,b_1 in k[x_1]. Comparing the constant coefficient in the relation a x_0+b x_1=0 gives b_0x_1=0 in k[x_1], hence b_0=0 because k[x_1] is a polynomial ring over the field k and therefore has no zero divisors. Thus b=x_0b_1.

source.place: proof of the Koszul resolution on the regular sequence x_0,x_1: exactness at the middle term

proof.text: Substituting b=x_0b_1 into the relation gives x_0(a+b_1x_1)=0 in S. The ring S=k[x_0,x_1] is an integral domain by [lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-ring-domain], so cancellation of the nonzero element x_0 yields a=-b_1x_1.

source.place: proof of the Koszul resolution on the regular sequence x_0,x_1: exactness at the middle term

proof.text: Set c=-b_1. Then a=c x_1 and b=-c x_0, which is the required description of every syzygy.
